source: Craft moves harvested from primary writing guidance (GOV.UK, digital.gov plain language, Google Search Central, Google/Microsoft style guides, NN/g, W3C, BBC/Netflix subtitle guides, Cialdini's IAW site) plus Wikipedia articles for named rhetorical and narrative devices; every URL status-checked 2026-10-04.

items.name: Social proof
items.one_line: Show that people like the reader already chose this (counts, reviews, logos, named users) so the choice feels safe.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Social proof / consensus is one of Cialdini's principles of persuasion

sources.title: Social proof (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and research background

items.note: Proof must be real and attributable; invented counts or reviews are a compliance issue (see comp: items), not a craft choice. Strongest when the proof-giver resembles the reader.

items.name: Authority proof
items.one_line: Borrow credibility from credentials, experts, certifications, media mentions or hard data placed where doubt peaks.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Authority is one of the seven principles

items.name: Reciprocity (give first)
items.one_line: Give genuine value before the ask (a useful tip, template, free sample) so the request lands as a fair exchange.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Reciprocity is one of the seven principles

sources.title: Reciprocity (social psychology) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: background on the norm

items.name: Micro-yes ladder (commitment and consistency)
items.one_line: Ask for a small, easy agreement first (a quiz answer, a reply, a free step) so the bigger ask feels consistent with it.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: consistency is activated by asking for small initial commitments

sources.title: Foot-in-the-door technique (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: small request first raises compliance with a larger one

items.name: Liking and shared identity
items.one_line: Make the writer likeable and signal shared identity (we-language, same city, same struggle) without faking it.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Liking and Unity are two of the seven principles

items.name: Ethical scarcity
items.one_line: State a real limit (stock, seats, batch size) plainly and specifically; never invent one.

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Scarcity is one of the seven principles

sources.title: Scarcity (social psychology) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: why perceived scarcity raises value

sources.title: FTC staff report: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
sources.supports: fake scarcity and urgency are treated as dark patterns

items.note: Fake low-stock or fake 'only 2 left' counters are dark patterns; pair with the relevant comp: items.

items.name: Ethical urgency (real deadlines)
items.one_line: Give a true reason to act now (a dated deadline, price change, cohort start) and say what happens after it.

sources.title: FTC staff report: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
sources.supports: fake countdown timers and false urgency are dark patterns

sources.title: Dark pattern (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: catalogue of manipulative urgency patterns to avoid

items.note: Countdown timers that reset, and 'today only' that runs every day, are the failure mode.

items.name: Price anchoring
items.one_line: Show a relevant higher reference first (cost of the problem, the premium tier, the alternative) so the price reads against it.

sources.title: Anchoring effect (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: first number seen biases later judgements

items.note: Anchor must be honest (a real list price or a real cost of inaction); fake 'was' prices are a compliance problem.

items.name: Decoy option
items.one_line: Add a clearly weaker third option next to the target plan so the target reads as the obvious pick.

sources.title: Decoy effect (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: an asymmetrically dominated option shifts preference

items.name: Loss-aversion framing
items.one_line: Frame the cost of not acting (what the reader keeps losing) alongside the gain, because losses weigh heavier.

sources.title: Loss aversion (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: losses loom larger than equivalent gains

sources.title: Framing effect (psychology) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: same facts framed as loss vs gain change choices

items.name: Curse-of-knowledge fix
items.one_line: Rewrite for someone who does not know what you know: define the term, add the missing step, show the example.

sources.title: Curse of knowledge (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: experts struggle to imagine not knowing

items.name: Testimonial placement
items.one_line: Put a specific, named testimonial right next to the claim or objection it proves, not in a block at the end.

sources.title: Testimonial (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a testimonial is in advertising

items.name: Risk reversal (guarantee)
items.one_line: Move the risk from buyer to seller with a clear, specific guarantee and say exactly how to claim it.

sources.title: Money-back guarantee (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a satisfaction guarantee is and why sellers use it

items.name: Call-to-action writing
items.one_line: One clear, verb-led instruction that names the action and the payoff, repeated where the reader is ready.

sources.title: Call to action (marketing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of a CTA

items.name: The P.S. line
items.one_line: Use a postscript after the sign-off to restate the offer, deadline or strongest benefit for readers who skip to the end.

sources.title: Postscript (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what a postscript is

items.name: Voice-of-customer mining
items.one_line: Lift the exact words customers use (reviews, support tickets, interviews, comments) and write the copy in them.

sources.title: Voice of the customer (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: capturing customers' expressed needs in their own terms

items.name: Show, don't tell
items.one_line: Replace a summary judgement ('she was nervous') with the action, detail or dialogue that lets the reader conclude it.

sources.title: Show, don't tell (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and origin of the guideline

items.name: In medias res opening
items.one_line: Start in the middle of the action and fill in the backstory later.

sources.title: In medias res (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: narrative opening in the middle of events

items.name: Foreshadowing (plant and payoff)
items.one_line: Plant a detail early that pays off later, and cut details that never pay off.

sources.title: Foreshadowing (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

sources.title: Chekhov's gun (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: every planted element should pay off

items.name: Callback
items.one_line: Bring back an earlier line, image or joke near the end so the piece feels closed and the reader feels rewarded.

sources.title: Callback (comedy) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a joke referring back to an earlier one

items.note: Covers both the story callback and the comic callback named in the brief.

items.name: Twist / reveal
items.one_line: Withhold one fact and reveal it late so the reader reinterprets everything before it.

sources.title: Plot twist (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and types of twist

items.name: Conflict and stakes
items.one_line: Give the story an obstacle and make clear what is lost if the character fails.

sources.title: Conflict (narrative) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: conflict as the engine of narrative

items.name: Sensory detail
items.one_line: Add one concrete sight, sound, smell, taste or touch to make a scene real in a few words.

sources.title: Imagery (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: sensory language evokes vivid impressions

items.name: Dialogue
items.one_line: Let people speak in short, real-sounding lines that reveal character or move the story, instead of reporting what they said.

sources.title: Dialogue (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: dialogue as a literary and dramatic form

items.name: Anecdote lead
items.one_line: Open with a short true story about one person, then widen to the point it illustrates.

sources.title: Lead paragraph (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: lead types in journalism, including feature-style leads

sources.title: Anecdote (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what an anecdote is

items.name: Nut graf
items.one_line: After a feature-style opening, add one paragraph that says why the story matters now.

sources.title: Nut graph (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: paragraph explaining the news value of a feature

items.name: Vulnerability / confession
items.one_line: Admit a real mistake, fear or failure before the lesson so the reader trusts the advice.

sources.title: Confessional writing (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the confessional mode in literature

items.note: The literary source is about the genre; the marketing use (a founder admitting a failure) is a craft extension. Fake vulnerability ('I cried when I hit 10k followers') reads as a tell.

items.name: Active voice
items.one_line: Put the doer first and the action in a verb ('We reviewed the claim', not 'The claim was reviewed').

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: use the active voice; it is more direct and keeps sentences short

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: Active voice
sources.supports: prefer active voice

sources.title: digital.gov plain language guide
sources.supports: US federal plain language guidance (plainlanguage.gov now redirects here)

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 10: use the active voice

items.name: Short sentences
items.one_line: Keep most sentences short and split the long ones; one idea per sentence.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: quote: 'Try to split up sentences that are over 25 words long.'

items.note: The 25-word split point is GOV.UK's; other houses differ. Pair with tech:sentence_rhythm so short does not become monotonous.

items.name: Rule of three
items.one_line: Group items in threes for rhythm and memorability; the third item carries the weight or the twist.

sources.title: Rule of three (writing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: triads are more satisfying and memorable

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: lists overuse of the rule of three as an AI tell

items.note: Reflexive triplets in every sentence are a listed AI tell; use once or twice per piece.

items.name: Parallelism
items.one_line: Give matching ideas matching grammar (same verb form, same shape) in lists, headings and contrasts.

sources.title: Parallelism (grammar) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: balance of grammatically similar constructions

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 15: express co-ordinate ideas in similar form

items.name: Antithesis
items.one_line: Set two opposed ideas side by side in balanced phrases to sharpen a point.

sources.title: Antithesis (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: juxtaposition of contrasting ideas in parallel structure

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: lists negative parallelism ('not X, but Y') as an AI tell

items.note: The formula 'It's not X, it's Y' is a listed AI tell when used reflexively.

items.name: Alliteration
items.one_line: Repeat an opening sound across nearby words to make a phrase stick (sparingly: headlines, taglines, names).

sources.title: Alliteration (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

items.name: Chiasmus
items.one_line: Reverse the order of key words in a second clause (AB, BA) for a memorable, quotable line.

sources.title: Chiasmus (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

items.name: Metaphor and analogy
items.one_line: Explain the unfamiliar through something the reader already knows, with one clear mapping.

sources.title: Metaphor (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

sources.title: Analogy (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: transfer of meaning from a known source to a target

items.name: Wordplay and puns
items.one_line: Use a double meaning or sound-alike for a smile, only where the brand voice allows and the meaning survives.

sources.title: Pun (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and types of pun

items.note: Puns often do not survive translation or Hinglish code-switching; test with a reader of the target language.

items.name: Rhetorical question
items.one_line: Ask a question the reader answers in their head, to pull them in or make a point land.

sources.title: Rhetorical question (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

items.note: GOV.UK advises against questions as headings because they are hard to frontload; keep rhetorical questions for body copy and hooks.

items.name: Anaphora and deliberate repetition
items.one_line: Repeat the same opening words across successive lines to build rhythm and emphasis.

sources.title: Anaphora (rhetoric) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: repetition at the start of successive clauses

sources.title: Epistrophe (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: repetition at the end of successive clauses

items.name: Punchline at the end of the line
items.one_line: Put the surprising or most important word last in the sentence, where emphasis naturally falls.

sources.title: Paraprosdokian (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a sentence whose latter part surprises and reframes the first

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 18: place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end

items.name: Plain language
items.one_line: Use common words, short sentences and a clear order so the intended reader understands on first read.

sources.title: digital.gov plain language guide
sources.supports: US federal plain language guidance

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: plain English rules for government content

sources.title: Plain language (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and history

items.name: Power words (loaded language)
items.one_line: Choose a few emotionally charged words at decision points; strip the ones that only inflate.

sources.title: Loaded language (Wikipedia; 'Power word' redirects here)
sources.supports: words with strong connotations used to influence an audience

items.note: Lists of 'power words' are marketing folklore; the device itself is loaded language. Overuse slides into hype and AI-style promotional vocabulary.

items.name: Contractions for a conversational voice
items.one_line: Use everyday contractions (you'll, it's) to sound human, but spell out negatives where misreading costs something.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: use contractions like 'you'll' but avoid negative contractions like 'can't' or 'don't'

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Use contractions
sources.supports: Microsoft recommends contractions for a friendly tone

items.note: GOV.UK and Microsoft disagree on negative contractions; follow the client's style guide.

items.name: Unhide verbs (fix nominalisations)
items.one_line: Turn nouns made from verbs back into verbs ('make a decision' to 'decide', 'conduct an analysis' to 'analyse').

sources.title: Nominalization (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: verbs and adjectives turned into nouns

items.name: Cut qualifiers, hedges and weasel words
items.one_line: Delete 'very', 'really', 'quite', 'some say' and unattributed claims; keep a hedge only where the uncertainty is real.

sources.title: Hedge (linguistics) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: hedges lessen the force of a statement

sources.title: Weasel word (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: vague attributions that create an impression of a claim

sources.title: Concision (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: eliminating redundancy while keeping meaning

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 13: omit needless words

items.name: Front-loading
items.one_line: Put the most important words at the start of every heading, link, bullet, sentence and paragraph.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Create a clear structure
sources.supports: frontload your content: put the most important information first

sources.title: NN/g: First 2 Words, a signal for the scanning eye
sources.supports: scanners read the first words of lines

items.name: Writing for the F-pattern
items.one_line: Assume readers scan the top and left edge; put meaning in headings, first lines and first words to beat the F-pattern.

sources.title: NN/g: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web
sources.supports: eyetracking finding and how to design text against it

sources.title: NN/g: Text Scanning Patterns
sources.supports: other scanning patterns (layer-cake, spotted, etc.)

items.name: Chunking
items.one_line: Break content into small, labelled groups (short paragraphs, lists, sections) so the reader can process and find it.

sources.title: NN/g: How Chunking Helps Content Processing
sources.supports: definition and methods

items.name: Conclusion-first paragraphs
items.one_line: Open each paragraph with its point (topic sentence), then support it, so skimmers get the message from first lines alone.

sources.title: NN/g: Inverted Pyramid
sources.supports: start with the conclusion, applies at page and paragraph level

sources.title: Topic sentence (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: topic sentence summarises the paragraph, usually first

sources.title: NN/g: Concise, Scannable, and Objective: How to Write for the Web
sources.supports: scanners read only first sentences; topic sentences and 'one idea per paragraph' matter

items.note: The whole-piece inverted pyramid is fw:inverted_pyramid (worker fw_hook); this item is the paragraph-level move.

items.name: Open loop
items.one_line: Raise a question or promise early and close it later, so the unfinished thread keeps the reader going.

sources.title: Zeigarnik effect (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: interrupted tasks are remembered better (the psychology usually cited for open loops)

items.note: The Zeigarnik research is about memory of interrupted tasks; its use for reading retention is a marketing extension. Every loop opened must close.

items.name: Cliffhanger
items.one_line: End a section, email or episode at an unresolved moment so the reader comes back for the next one.

sources.title: Cliffhanger (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

items.name: Descriptive subheads
items.one_line: Write headings that say what the section tells the reader, so the headings alone summarise the piece.

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: Headings
sources.supports: heading guidance

sources.title: NN/g: Formatting long-form content
sources.supports: headings and formatting help users scan long pages

items.name: Bulleted and numbered lists
items.one_line: Turn a run of parallel items or steps into a list; number steps, bullet unordered items, keep each item parallel.

sources.title: Google developer documentation style guide: Lists
sources.supports: when to use numbered vs bulleted lists

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Scannable content
sources.supports: lists and headings for scannability

items.name: Bold for skimmers
items.one_line: Bold a few key phrases that carry the meaning on their own; never whole sentences or every other line.

sources.title: NN/g: Formatting long-form content
sources.supports: bolding and formatting to support scanning

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: overuse of boldface is a listed AI tell

items.name: Title tag writing
items.one_line: Write a unique, descriptive, concise page title that says what the page is; avoid keyword stuffing and boilerplate.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Influencing your title links
sources.supports: Google's best practices for title elements

items.name: Meta description writing
items.one_line: Write a unique, specific summary of the page for each URL; Google may show it as the snippet but can also choose page text.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Control your snippets in search results
sources.supports: meta description best practices and that snippets can come from page content

items.name: Image alt text writing
items.one_line: Describe what the image shows and why it is there, in context; empty alt for purely decorative images.

sources.title: W3C WAI: An alt Decision Tree
sources.supports: how to decide what alt text an image needs

sources.title: Google Search Central: Image SEO best practices
sources.supports: descriptive alt text helps Google understand images

items.name: Descriptive anchor text (internal links)
items.one_line: Make link text say where the link goes ('2026 GST rate table', not 'click here'), concise and relevant to the target.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Link best practices
sources.supports: write good, descriptive anchor text

sources.title: GOV.UK: Write effective links
sources.supports: link text should describe the destination

sources.title: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)
sources.supports: link purpose must be clear from the link text or its context

items.name: First-hand experience signals (E-E-A-T)
items.one_line: Show you actually did, used or visited the thing: original photos, test results, specific numbers, who wrote it and why.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: asks whether content demonstrates first-hand expertise; Who, How and Why questions

items.name: Substantive freshness updates
items.one_line: Update a page by changing what is out of date (facts, prices, screenshots) and say what changed; never just bump the date.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: warns against changing page dates to seem fresh when content has not substantially changed

sources.title: GOV.UK: Write change notes
sources.supports: telling users what changed on an updated page

sources.title: Google Search Central: Influence your byline dates
sources.supports: how Google reads visible and structured publication / updated dates

items.name: Answer-first paragraph
items.one_line: Under a question-shaped heading, answer it directly in the first one or two sentences, then expand.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Featured snippets
sources.supports: how featured snippets are drawn from page text

sources.title: Google Search Central: AI features and your website
sources.supports: no additional requirements or special optimisation for AI Overviews / AI Mode; standard SEO best practices apply

items.note: Google states there is no special optimisation for AI Overviews; answer-first writing is a clarity move that also suits snippets. Claims that it 'guarantees' AI citations are unsourced.

items.name: FAQ block
items.one_line: Answer real follow-up questions in a short Q-and-A section at the end of a page, in the reader's own wording.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Latest documentation updates
sources.supports: FAQ rich result deprecated: no longer appears in Google Search starting May 7, 2026; docs removed June 2026

items.note: Since May 2026 FAQ markup no longer produces a Google rich result; write FAQs for readers (and answer extraction), not for the rich result.

items.name: Structure-friendly formatting
items.one_line: Present steps, specs, prices and Q&A as real headings, lists and tables so machines and skimmers can parse them.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Introduction to structured data
sources.supports: how structured data describes page content

sources.title: Google Search Central: AI features and your website
sources.supports: no special schema.org structured data is needed for AI features

items.name: Natural keyword placement
items.one_line: Use the words people search with in the title, main heading, opening and link text, naturally and never stuffed.

sources.title: Google Search Central: SEO Starter Guide
sources.supports: anticipate the words users search with; keyword stuffing is against spam policies

items.name: Captions and subtitle writing
items.one_line: Write on-video captions as short, well-timed lines broken at natural phrase boundaries, edited for reading speed.

sources.title: BBC Subtitle Guidelines
sources.supports: line-break, timing and length guidance; two lines maximum recommended for landscape/square video

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: industry subtitle style rules

items.name: Ethical comment prompt
items.one_line: End with a genuine, specific question people want to answer, not 'comment YES' or 'tag a friend' bait.

sources.title: Meta: Fighting Engagement Bait on Facebook (2017)
sources.supports: Facebook demotes posts that goad people into likes, shares and comments

items.note: Engagement bait is demoted on Facebook per Meta's 2017 announcement; other platforms' current treatment needs checking per platform.

items.name: Writing for voice-over
items.one_line: Write for the ear: short spoken sentences, one idea per breath, numbers and names written the way they are said.

sources.title: Voice-over (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: what voice-over narration is

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS WC193: News Writing for Television and Radio
sources.supports: read the story aloud; broadcast rules for writing and rounding numbers

sources.title: Media Helping Media: Writing a radio news script
sources.supports: practical rules for writing news copy to be spoken

items.name: Personalisation tokens
items.one_line: Insert merge fields (name, city, last purchase) only where they add meaning, always with a safe fallback value.

sources.title: Mailchimp: All the Merge Tags Cheat Sheet
sources.supports: how merge tags insert subscriber data

sources.title: Mail merge (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition

items.name: Subject line + preheader pairing
items.one_line: Write the preheader as the second half of the subject line: it extends or pays off the subject instead of repeating it.

sources.title: Litmus: The ultimate guide to preview text
sources.supports: what preview text is and how clients display it

items.note: Character counts for preview text belong to plat:email_subject / platform items.

items.name: Error-message structure
items.one_line: Say what went wrong in plain words, why if useful, and exactly how to fix it, next to the problem, without blame.

sources.title: NN/g: Error-Message Guidelines
sources.supports: visibility, communication and efficiency guidelines for error messages

items.name: Empty-state copy
items.one_line: When a screen has no data yet, say why it is empty and give the one action that fills it.

sources.title: NN/g: Designing Empty States in Complex Applications
sources.supports: empty states should communicate status, teach and offer a direct path

items.name: Progressive disclosure
items.one_line: Show only what most readers need now; tuck detail behind a link, toggle or later step.

sources.title: NN/g: Progressive Disclosure
sources.supports: defer advanced or rarely used information

items.name: Consistent terminology
items.one_line: Call one thing by one name everywhere (UI, help, emails); keep a word list and do not vary terms for style.

sources.title: NN/g: Consistency and Standards (usability heuristic #4)
sources.supports: users should not wonder whether different words mean the same thing

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: elegant variation (swapping synonyms for the same thing) is a listed tell

items.name: Swipe file
items.one_line: Keep a collection of proven ads, emails and lines to study structure and moves, never to copy wording.

sources.title: Swipe file (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: collection of tested copy kept for reference

items.name: SME interview
items.one_line: Interview a subject-matter expert with prepared questions to get the specifics, stories and quotes no desk research gives.

sources.title: Subject-matter expert (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: who an SME is

items.name: Outlining
items.one_line: Plan the sections and their points as a hierarchy before drafting; fix order and gaps at outline stage.

sources.title: Outline (list) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: hierarchical outline as a writing plan

items.name: Freewriting
items.one_line: Write nonstop for a set time without editing to get raw material and find what you think.

sources.title: Free writing (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and method

items.name: Features to benefits
items.one_line: Translate each feature (what it is) into the outcome it gives the reader (what it does for them), and lead with the outcome.

sources.title: Copyblogger: Copywriting 101 (ebook)
sources.supports: move past what a product is to what it does for the buyer

items.name: The 'So what?' test
items.one_line: After every claim ask 'so what?' until the answer is something the reader actually cares about; write that answer.

sources.title: Handcart Media: the 'So what' test for website copy
sources.supports: practitioner description of the test (secondary, low confidence)

items.note: Folk technique with no single originator; search summaries attach conversion-lift numbers to it that are unsourced, do not repeat them.

items.name: Objection handling in copy
items.one_line: List the reader's likely reasons not to act and answer each one where it arises (inline, FAQ, guarantee, 'even if' line).

sources.title: Copyhackers: The 3 essential copywriting techniques
sources.supports: 'even if' technique: promise + 'even if' + the objection

sources.title: Joanna Wiebe: The Conversion Marketer's Guide to Landing Page Copywriting (Unbounce)
sources.supports: work backward from the goal through the objections and anxieties that block conversion

items.note: Objections come from VOC research (tech:voice_of_customer_mining), not guesswork.

items.name: Reason-why ('because')
items.one_line: Give the reader a real reason for every claim and request, joined with 'because'; a stated reason makes compliance more likely.

sources.title: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz (1978), The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action, JPSP 36(6)
sources.supports: copier study: requests with a reason, even a placebic one, got more compliance for small requests

sources.title: Full text of the 1978 copier study (hosted copy)
sources.supports: the effect of a placebic reason disappeared when the request was larger

items.note: The empty-'because' effect only held for a small favour; for bigger asks the reason must be real. Do not cite the study as proof that any 'because' works.

items.name: Future pacing
items.one_line: Walk the reader through a specific moment after they have the result, in present tense, so the outcome feels concrete.

sources.title: How to use future pacing to help your prospect imagine a better life (Medium)
sources.supports: practitioner description; term borrowed from NLP (secondary, low confidence) [403 to scripted fetch; URL seen in search results 2026-10-04]

items.note: The term comes from NLP, which has weak scientific support; treat it as a craft move, not a proven mechanism. Never future-pace results the product cannot deliver.

items.name: Unique mechanism
items.one_line: Name and explain the specific method that makes the result possible, so a sceptical reader believes this one is different.

sources.title: Todd Brown: What's your product's unique mechanism?
sources.supports: definition; promotes the process rather than the result (page refused a scripted status check; seen via search)

sources.title: Unique selling proposition (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the older USP concept the mechanism builds on

items.note: Concept credited to Eugene Schwartz (Breakthrough Advertising, 1966), popularised by Todd Brown; the mechanism must be true and explainable.

items.name: Big idea
items.one_line: Build the whole piece around one fresh, simple central idea that makes the offer memorable and different.

sources.title: Big Idea (marketing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition and Ogilvy association

sources.title: CopyChief: WANTED, the Big Idea (direct response style)
sources.supports: how direct-response writers use the big idea

items.name: Write to one reader
items.one_line: Picture one specific person and write to them as 'you', not to an audience or 'users'.

sources.title: Express Writers: 57 pieces of copywriting advice
sources.supports: 'write to one person, not a million', attributed to Fairfax M. Cone (secondary, low confidence)

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use the right tone
sources.supports: address the user directly as 'you'

items.name: Match copy to awareness level
items.one_line: Decide whether the reader is unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware or most aware, and open where they are.

sources.title: Eugene Schwartz 5 levels of awareness explained (Selzee)
sources.supports: summary of the five levels from Breakthrough Advertising (1966) (secondary)

items.note: Originates in Eugene Schwartz, Breakthrough Advertising (1966), cited by name. Could also be filed as a framework (fw_hook worker); merge decides.

items.name: Specificity
items.one_line: Replace vague claims with exact, checkable details (numbers, names, places, times) the reader can picture and believe.

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 12: use definite, specific, concrete language

items.note: Every specific must be true and sourced; an invented exact number is worse than a vague one.

items.name: Pain agitation
items.one_line: Make the reader feel the cost of the problem with concrete consequences before offering the fix, without fearmongering.

sources.title: Copyhackers: Copywriting formulas, the ultimate guide
sources.supports: agitation as the middle step of problem-agitate-solve formulas

items.note: The whole PAS structure is fw:pas (worker fw_hook); this is the agitation move alone. Agitation about health, money or safety can tip into unfair fear appeals (see comp: items).

items.name: But / therefore links
items.one_line: Join story beats with 'but' or 'therefore' (cause and complication), never 'and then', so events drive each other.

sources.title: Aerogramme Studio: Writing advice from South Park's Trey Parker and Matt Stone
sources.supports: the 'but/therefore' rule from their NYU class visit

sources.title: Writing Advice from Matt Stone & Trey Parker @ NYU (video)
sources.supports: primary recording of the advice

items.name: Character with a want
items.one_line: Give the person in the story a clear desire and an obstacle, so the reader has something to root for.

sources.title: Protagonist (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the protagonist as the character whose goals drive the story

sources.title: Character arc (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: change a character undergoes in pursuing a goal

items.note: In brand stories the customer is the character with the want, not the brand.

items.name: Sentence-length rhythm
items.one_line: Mix short, medium and long sentences so the prose has music; land key points on a short one after longer ones.

sources.title: Aerogramme Studio: Gary Provost on varying sentence length
sources.supports: Provost's demonstration that varied sentence length creates rhythm

sources.title: Gary Provost (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: author of 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing (1985)

sources.title: Hemingway Editor: Readability
sources.supports: save longer sentences for emphasis or variety and rhythm; do not chase conciseness at all costs

items.note: Provost's passage is copyrighted; cite by name, do not paste it.

items.name: Concrete nouns and strong verbs
items.one_line: Prefer nouns you can picture and verbs that carry the action over abstract nouns plus weak verbs and adjectives.

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 12: use definite, specific, concrete language

sources.title: Nominalization (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: abstract nouns made from verbs weaken prose

items.name: Positive form
items.one_line: Say what is, not what is not ('forgot', not 'did not remember'); avoid double negatives.

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 11: put statements in positive form

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use clear language
sources.supports: negative contractions are often misread as the opposite

items.name: Bucket brigades
items.one_line: Short conversational bridge phrases ('Here's why.' 'The catch?') that carry the reader over a paragraph break.

sources.title: Copyhackers: How to engage with the bucket brigade technique
sources.supports: definition and use

sources.title: Backlinko: Copywriting, 7 fundamentals
sources.supports: Brian Dean's use of bucket brigades in blog posts

items.note: Overuse reads as formula; several stock bucket-brigade openers ('Here's the thing') overlap with AI-tell lists (see pcw.py AI_TELLS).

items.name: Transitions
items.one_line: Signal the logical link between sentences and paragraphs (contrast, cause, example, sequence) so the reader never wonders why the next part follows.

sources.title: UNC Writing Center: Transitions
sources.supports: how transitions express logical relationships

items.note: Stacked transition words ('Moreover', 'Furthermore', 'Additionally') are a common AI tell; the logic should carry the link.

items.name: One-idea and one-sentence paragraphs
items.one_line: Keep one idea per paragraph and use an occasional one-sentence paragraph for emphasis or a turn.

sources.title: NN/g: Concise, Scannable, and Objective: How to Write for the Web
sources.supports: the 'one idea per paragraph' rule observed in user testing

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 8: make the paragraph the unit of composition

items.note: A page made only of one-line paragraphs (LinkedIn 'broetry') loses the emphasis it was after.

items.name: You-focus (second person)
items.one_line: Address the reader as 'you' and make them the subject of sentences; cut 'we offer' sentences that are about the writer.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Use the right tone
sources.supports: address the user as 'you' where possible

sources.title: GOV.UK A to Z style guide
sources.supports: address the user as 'you'; avoid gendered pronouns

items.name: Numbers as numerals (for reading)
items.one_line: On screen, write numbers as numerals so they stand out to scanners; in scripts for the ear, write them the way they are said.

sources.title: GOV.UK A to Z style guide
sources.supports: write all other numbers in numerals (including 2 to 9) except in common expressions

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS WC193: News Writing for Television and Radio
sources.supports: broadcast number style differs: spell out small numbers and round large ones

items.note: House styles differ (AP spells out one to nine); follow the client's style guide.

items.name: TL;DR / key-takeaways summary
items.one_line: Open long pieces with a short summary or takeaways box that states what the reader will learn or must do.

sources.title: GOV.UK: Write clear summaries
sources.supports: how to write a page summary that tells users what the page is for

items.name: Slippery slide
items.one_line: Make every element do one job: the headline gets the first line read, the first line gets the second read, and so on to the CTA.

sources.title: Upgrow: Joe Sugarman's slippery slide
sources.supports: summary of Sugarman's concept from The Adweek Copywriting Handbook (secondary) [403 to scripted fetch; URL seen in search results 2026-10-04]

sources.title: Joseph Sugarman - Wikipedia
sources.supports: Direct-response copywriter, founder of JS&A and BluBlocker

sources.title: The Adweek Copywriting Handbook - Goodreads
sources.supports: Sugarman's book where the slippery-slide idea is set out

items.note: Originator: Joseph Sugarman, The Adweek Copywriting Handbook; cited by name. [merged from fw:slippery_slide: Joseph Sugarman, The Adweek Copywriting Handbook (book). Borderline with technique (tech:bucket_brigade lives with tech_edit).]

items.name: Pattern interrupt
items.one_line: Break the expected pattern (a sudden short line, a visual change, an unexpected question) at the point attention usually drops.

sources.title: YouTube Help: Measure key moments for audience retention
sources.supports: dips show where viewers skip or leave, i.e. where an interrupt is needed

items.note: No primary source defines the copy technique (the term comes from NLP); the YouTube report only shows where attention drops. Low confidence.

items.name: Search-intent matching
items.one_line: Work out what the searcher wants to do (know, do, go somewhere, visit in person) and give that format first.

sources.title: Google: Search Quality Rater Guidelines, an overview
sources.supports: how raters judge whether results meet the user's need/intent

sources.title: User intent (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: types of search intent

items.name: Topic and entity coverage
items.one_line: Cover the sub-questions, related entities and terms a complete answer needs, so the page fully satisfies the topic.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: asks whether the content gives a substantial, complete or comprehensive description of the topic

sources.title: Semantic search (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: search engines matching meaning and entities, not only keywords

items.note: Coverage means answering what readers need, not padding to match competitor word counts.

items.name: Descriptive URL slug
items.one_line: Use short, readable words in the URL that describe the page, not IDs or dates that will go stale.

sources.title: Google Search Central: URL structure best practices
sources.supports: use simple, descriptive words in URLs

items.name: First line above the fold
items.one_line: Make the opening line of a post or caption complete and compelling on its own, because the rest hides behind 'see more'.

sources.title: NN/g: First 2 Words, a signal for the scanning eye
sources.supports: readers decide from the first words whether to continue

sources.title: LinkedIn Help: Post and share updates
sources.supports: how posts are composed and displayed

items.note: Truncation lengths per platform belong to plat: items; hook families belong to hook: items (worker fw_hook).

items.name: Line breaks for mobile reading
items.one_line: Break captions and emails into short lines and short paragraphs with white space so they read on a phone screen.

sources.title: NN/g: Reading Content on Mobile Devices
sources.supports: comprehension research on small screens; difficult content suffers most on mobile

items.name: Native formatting per platform
items.one_line: Format for how the platform actually renders text (no markdown where it shows literally, platform-native lists, mentions, emoji bullets) rather than pasting one version everywhere.
items.note: Unsourced craft norm; what each platform renders is documented per plat: item (formatting field).

items.name: Hashtag selection
items.one_line: Use a few specific, relevant hashtags that describe the content, not long lists of generic ones.

sources.title: Later: Instagram hashtags guide
sources.supports: practitioner guidance on fewer, relevant hashtags (secondary)

items.note: Search results report Instagram enforcing a cap on hashtags per post from Dec 2025; that is a platform limit to verify in plat: items, not here.

items.name: Retention re-hooks
items.one_line: Plant a new reason to keep watching at the points viewers usually drop (a tease, a question, a stakes reminder), not only at the start.

sources.title: YouTube Help: Measure key moments for audience retention
sources.supports: intro, top moments, spikes and dips; intro measures how many still watch after the first 30 seconds

items.name: On-screen text vs voice-over split
items.one_line: Do not put the full VO on screen; use on-screen text for short keywords, numbers and labels that support what is said.

sources.title: Devlin Peck: Mayer's principles of multimedia learning
sources.supports: redundancy principle: graphics + narration beat graphics + narration + identical text; short labels can help

sources.title: Revising the Redundancy Principle in Multimedia Learning (paper)
sources.supports: short redundant on-screen phrases can aid retention [403 to scripted fetch; URL seen in search results 2026-10-04]

items.note: The research is about learning material; social videos watched muted need captions anyway (tech:captions_subtitles).

items.name: Loopable ending
items.one_line: Write the last line so it flows back into the first, inviting an immediate rewatch of a short video.
items.note: No primary source found within budget; YouTube's retention report shows rewatched moments as spikes but does not describe loops. Low confidence.

items.name: Single-CTA email
items.one_line: Give each email one job and one call to action, repeated if needed, instead of several competing links.

sources.title: Call to action (marketing) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of a CTA

items.note: Conversion-lift figures quoted online for single-CTA emails were not traced to a primary; leave numbers out.

items.name: Plain-text style email
items.one_line: Write some emails like a personal note (no heavy design, one link, a person's name in the signature) where it suits the relationship.

sources.title: Litmus: A/B testing HTML vs plain text emails
sources.supports: Litmus's own test: results differed by audience (customers vs non-customers)

sources.title: Litmus: Best practices for plain text emails
sources.supports: why and how to write the plain-text version

items.note: One company's test, not a law; test on your own list (edit:ab_test_copy).

items.name: Sender-name choice
items.one_line: Use a recognisable, consistent from-name (a person at the brand, or the brand) that matches the email's content.

sources.title: Mailchimp: Email sender name best practices
sources.supports: recognisable, consistent, brand-including sender names

items.name: Front-loaded button labels
items.one_line: Label buttons with a specific verb phrase that says what happens ('Save draft', 'Pay ₹499'), not 'OK' or 'Submit'.

sources.title: NN/g: UI Copy, guidelines for command names
sources.supports: command labels should be specific and start with the important word

items.name: Form labels and helper text
items.one_line: Use a visible label for every field and put format hints in helper text, not in placeholder text that disappears.

sources.title: NN/g: Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful
sources.supports: placeholder text as labels hurts usability

items.name: Confirmation-dialog copy
items.one_line: Ask only before destructive or costly actions, state the consequence, and label the buttons with the actual actions.

sources.title: NN/g: Confirmation Dialogs Can Prevent User Errors (If Not Overused)
sources.supports: when to use confirmation dialogs and how to word them

items.name: Step-by-step instructions
items.one_line: Write procedures as numbered steps, one action per step, starting with the goal or location and an imperative verb.

sources.title: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: Writing step-by-step instructions
sources.supports: rules for procedures

items.name: Zero draft (permission to write badly)
items.one_line: Get a complete rough version down fast without editing, then revise; separate drafting from judging.

sources.title: Poynter: The power of awful first drafts
sources.supports: case for fast, imperfect first drafts in journalism

items.note: Popularised by Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird (1994), cited by name.

items.name: Headline-first writing
items.one_line: Write many candidate headlines before (and after) drafting; the chosen promise defines what the body must deliver.

sources.title: Headline (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: role of the headline

sources.title: Nieman Lab (2023): study of Upworthy's headline A/B tests
sources.supports: Upworthy routinely wrote and tested several headlines per story

items.note: Headline families themselves are hook: items (worker fw_hook).

items.name: Read it aloud
items.one_line: Read the draft out loud to catch clumsy rhythm, missing words and sentences too long to say in one breath.

sources.title: UF/IFAS EDIS WC193: News Writing for Television and Radio
sources.supports: reading the story aloud is the most important habit when writing for the ear

items.name: Writing to a word budget
items.one_line: Allot words to each section before drafting (from the brief's length) and cut to the budget instead of trimming at random.
items.note: Unsourced craft norm; per-genre lengths live in genre cards and platform limits in plat: items.
